lines: My fingers will not bend in this cold any more. So I have taken up talking instead.
My mother's spoon is bent and has been bent for sixty years. It is still a spoon.
I have outlived three roofs and two of them were better built than this one.
Sit down. Everybody your age is always going somewhere and it never turns out to be anywhere.
The bread was better when the flour was worse. I have thought about that for years and it holds.
I do one useful thing a day now. Today it was the onions. Tomorrow it may be nothing.
There is a knack to that latch. Everybody says there is a knack and nobody will fix the latch.
I sleep badly and then I sleep at noon and everybody acts as though that is a new development.
That dog has been coming to my door for nine years and it is not my dog and I do not feed it.
I feed it. Obviously I feed it. Nine years.
I have been telling the same four stories for thirty years and I have noticed you all mouthing along.
Wind is coming round tonight. My knee is more reliable than anybody's tide table and less popular.
There is a way to coil that rope and it is not the way you are doing it. Come here.
I taught half this village to swim and the other half taught themselves badly.
When I say it was better before, I mean the bread. Only the bread. Do not put words in my mouth.
My hands did that gate. Look at the joint. Sixty years and it has not dropped a finger's width.
Everybody keeps asking if I need anything. What I need is for people to stop asking me that.
A hand's width a year. That is all it is. That is the whole monster, a hand's width a year.
I have moved twice. My mother moved once. My grandmother did not move at all and did not need to.
I remember a coastline that stayed where you left it. You will not get that from anybody younger.
That was a street. There, where it is flat. I could walk you down it with my eyes shut.
The salt gets into the wells first, then the gardens, then the houses. Always that order. Always.
We say the level because the other word is too big to say four times a day. That is all that is.
Nobody notices it rising. You notice one morning that a step you used to sit on is a step you dive to.
The frogs go up a year ahead of the people. They always have. They are simply better at it.
I marked the door post as a girl and my daughter marks it now and the marks only ever go up.
We are not survivors. Survivors ran. We are the descendants of the ones who could not be bothered.
There is a road under there, straight as anything, going down and down and not stopping.
Do not build anything you love below the third post. I have said that to four generations now.
Every family here has a house their grandparents built that you would need a boat to knock on.
The bottom row goes first. It has always gone first. It simply used to be a long way further out.
You can tell somebody's age here by which move they call the recent one.
I have watched this happen slowly enough to be bored by it, which nobody warns you about.
There is a door down there I could find blindfolded. I have not been down to it in eleven years.
My knees, before you ask. Not sentiment. My knees.
There is a key on my nail for a house that has been underwater since my daughter was small.
I keep it because taking it off the nail would be a decision and I am not making any more of those.
The bell in the old hall is still down there. People claim to hear it. They do not. I understand why they say it.
Vell's wife sang while she gutted fish, in a voice like a gull with a grievance, and I can still hear it.
The ledger has her house, her year, and what they saved. It does not have the singing. Nobody was measuring that.
We eat off a door taken from a drowned house. It is a good door. It was always a good door.
I can name every family from the low street in order and I do it when I cannot sleep.
It takes about forty names to get me under. That is a useful thing to know about yourself.
There is a garden gate down there still shut. Somebody shut it on the way out. I know who.
My brother is under the plum on the hill. He carried the stones up in his coat and then did not see it fruit.
A shoe came up in the shallows last spring. A child's. Everybody went quiet and then everybody carried on.
The names last about two generations past the places, and then they go as well, and that is the real drowning.
I have a bowl with a blue bird on it out of a kitchen I was never invited into. We use it daily.
Two letters and a heart cut into a beam. He is dead, she is dead, the beam is underwater, and it is still there.
The markers were built by people who knew this was coming. That is what we tell each other.
It is almost certainly not true. It is also why two families on this hill get out of bed. Weigh that.
The great wall was a dam and it failed. So the walkers go looking for the place where it failed.
There is no place. Not hidden, not lost. There is simply nothing to find. I have never said so to one of them.
The ring of arches was a cistern, and we tell children lions drank there, and I told my children that.
The carved city was cut out of rock rather than built, and so it is held to be older than the water.
Which would mean there was a before. That is what every one of those arguments is actually about.
The calendar stone is supposed to say when it stops. It has been read a thousand ways. It says nothing.
Build like the mountain terraces and you live. That is uplander religion and it is a decent religion.
The tomb is for one person and it is the most beautiful thing there is and nobody argues about the tomb.
Everything else in this world is a fight. The tomb just gets agreed with. I have never got over that.
Nobody knows who built any of it. Everybody speaks as though they do. Both true, at once, forever.
Somebody chalked a marker line on the mill wall. As if chalk. As if chalk would do it.
I did not rub it off. You do not rub off the thing that got a family through the winter.
The wall-walkers come through for salt. Always limping, always going straight back out. Always salt.
Seven things still standing and everything ordinary underneath. People take that extremely personally.
The wrong stories are holding the roof up. I would not care to be the one who pulled one out.
Somebody has to be able to read this in fifty years. That is the whole of it. That is the entire plan.
They keep asking when I will move. I say I am waiting for a sign. There is no sign.
There is a well going salty and a daughter up the path, and one of those will win in the end.
We are teaching everyone letters now. Everyone. Including me, at my age, which is humiliating and correct.
The seeds at the back of the cold chamber are sealed with wax and they are not for us.
Ask me who they are for. Go on. Then we will both have to sit with the answer.
There is a shelf in the cave, planed smooth, pegged in, empty, built to the size of books.
Somebody measured a future and then made furniture for it. I do not know whether to laugh at that.
Devi planted the whole row knowing she goes before it fruits. Somebody will come through hungry, she said.
That is the closest thing to an argument I have heard in a year, and it was said over a spade.
Half of them want to go higher and half want to stay. Both halves are right. That is the trouble.
We cut names into stone now instead of writing them on paper. That is a decision about how long.
The songs carry the place names on purpose, so the names outlive the places. That is not an accident.
I am training the one who will do this after me and I have not told her that is what is happening.
She knows. She has known for a year. Neither of us is going to say it and that is how it should be.
Nobody here is trying to fix it. We are trying to hand it over intact. That is a different job.
The old ones apologise at the end. All of us do. I have decided I am going to try not to.
I will probably apologise. Everybody says they will not and then everybody does.
Bail, mend, bail. I did that for fifty years and now I watch other people do it badly.
Rope goes furry at the waterline and furry means replace. Tightening furry rope is how you lose a hand.
The boards kill you when they have dried and got wet again, not when they are simply wet.
Do not carry two things on the outside walkway. That is not advice. Two people, that rule cost.
Everything out here is tied to something else. That is either wisdom or it is just rope. Both, probably.
The tide table is not a suggestion, and I have been saying that since before your mother.
The knot outlives the hand that ties it. That is a saying and it is also literally true, look at that one.
I could tie that one-handed in the dark in a swell. I can barely tie it now, sitting down, in daylight.
Fifty years of fish. I would like it noted that I never once complained where the children could hear.
Every house here stands on legs and the legs get longer each time somebody rebuilds them.
You can date a house by the rungs on its ladder. Mine had four when I moved in. Count them now.
There were four rows out past this one when I was a girl. Four. Now there is us and then the sea.
At the big tides the water comes over the boards and everyone lifts their feet and keeps talking.
The uplanders call us stubborn and we call them cowards and neither side quite means it.
You can see roofs under us on a still day. I stopped finding that strange about fifty years ago.
We are the last row. The last row has always been somebody. It used to be people I knew.
Nobody out here says flood. We say the level. That is not denial, that is just how often we have to say it.
At the lowest tide the schoolyard railing comes up like a row of teeth. I sat behind that railing.
The children dare each other to touch it. I have watched three generations do that exact dare.
I was born in a room that is under where we are standing. Under. I could put my hand on the spot.
The old well is down there full of sea water, which everybody calls a joke and I have stopped laughing at.
We swim to the shrine ledge on her birthday and leave something and it is gone by morning.
Nineteen years knowing it washes off. That is not stupidity. That is the entire point of doing it.
I could find any doorway under this village by feel, in the dark. I have had to, twice, and I would rather not again.
The bricks down there are older and a different colour and nobody has made that colour in my lifetime.
Anzu ties on to a chimney out there. It was her aunt's chimney. I helped build the chimney.
We float over houses I helped roof and argue about a carved city none of us will ever stand in front of.
Somebody chalked a marker line on the mill. Meaning it stops there. It stops nowhere, and I let it stand.
The wall-walkers stop here for salt and not one of them can swim. Not one, in sixty years of them.
They walk a wall looking for a hole. We bail a house. Everybody picks something to be doing.
The ring of arches held water in on purpose and we hold water out on purpose and nobody finds that funny but me.
The uplanders say build like the mountain terraces. You cannot terrace open water. I have said that to their faces.
Everyone here agrees the tomb is the most beautiful thing there is and not one of us has seen it.
The markers stand on dry land and we stand on sticks. That comes up in every argument, eventually, always.
Some go up in the spring and some do not, and the two halves have stopped eating together, and that is worse than the water.
We teach them to swim before they can properly walk. Nobody says out loud why we do that.
We bail until we cannot bail and then we go. Not one season before. I have said that in front of everybody.
Which means I cannot take it back now, which is precisely why I said it in front of everybody.
The names of the drowned houses are going into a roof beam, cut deep, so the beam carries them out.
The children must know these walkways in the dark, in wind, by heart. That is not a chore. That is a plan.
Good rope on the ladder, whatever is left for everything else. That is new and it means something.
Somebody asked how long this row has got and the whole room suddenly had jobs to be doing.
One of these children will close this place up. I know which one. I have known since she was four.
Three doors in this village still shut properly and I could take you to all three with my eyes closed.
The gulls take anything you set down for one second. Sixty years and they have never once been slower.
The bell on the post is for weather. Rung four times in my life. Right four times.
A family left a whole set of pots when they went and we simply started using them. Nobody discussed it.
The sea rubs the broken glass soft and hands it back. It is the only courteous thing it does.
The sand gets in whatever you do. People still shout about it. I have stopped, which is progress.
That cart has had no wheels since before my son was born and my son has grey in his beard.
Boats tie where carts used to turn. There is a ring in the wall for each of those and both rings are still there.
The road out goes downhill, then into the water, then it stops being a road at all.
One family a year goes from the bottom row to the top. Nobody has ever gone back down. Not once.
You can tell how long a house has been empty by how far the weeds have got up the door.
There is a dark line at the same height on every wall in this village. That is where it gets to now.
The beach was twice this wide when I was small. I walked on the half that is gone. I remember the sand.
This place has been halfway through leaving for longer than most of the people in it have been alive.
Waiting on the calendar, people say, before we move again. That is a way of not deciding and we all know it.
The house on the corner still has its curtains up. I helped hang them. Nobody has lived there in eleven years.
There is a boat in the weeds with a family name on it. That family is three villages up and doing well.
I stand in the empty street sometimes and do nothing at all and then I come back in and put the kettle on.
We took the door off my parents' house and it is the table. We have eaten off their front door for thirty years.
A child's height is scratched up a doorframe at number four, going up and up, and then it stops.
There is a doll in that window and everybody has silently agreed that it stays in that window.
The bakery oven still stands in the ruin. People claim they can smell it. They cannot. I let them have it.
I will not walk the bottom lane. I go the long way round. I have gone the long way round for twenty years.
A wall-walker came through doing the whole length, looking for the break. His feet were ruined.
They never stop properly. I have offered a bed to about forty of them and about two took it.
The markers are said to show where it stops, which would mean somebody knew, which is a lovely thought.
Every roof beam here is cut to the mountain terrace angle. Supposedly. Nobody in living memory has measured.
Pilgrims go to the calendar stone, come back saying it said nothing, and go again the next year.
My brother argued the carved city predates the water, and therefore the world had a before, and he was right.
He was also unbearable about it for forty years and I miss him more than I can tell you.
We tell children lions drank at the ring of arches. I told mine. They told theirs. Nobody has seen a lion.
The tomb is the only one nobody fights about. Eighty years and I have never worked out what that means.
They are taking the good beams out of the empty houses before the sea gets them, and they are right to.
It feels like robbing. It is not robbing. I still cannot watch it, so I go and sit round the back.
The families who went up send word back and the word is always the same word. Come up.
My son is teaching his boy to mend a roof they will not be living under. They both know it.
They finished it properly anyway. I watched the whole thing from that step and said nothing.
This year's trees went in on the high ground instead of the garden. Nobody announced that. It was a decision.
Somebody is listing everything abandoned here so it is at least written down somewhere, by somebody.
There is talk of carrying the bell up the hill. Moving the bell would make it official and everybody knows it.
I have moved once and once is enough for one life. I am aware how that sounds. I am not moving.
Nine terraces, both sides, by hand. I did that for forty years and now I supervise, badly.
Everything up here is carried up. Including the water. Including me, one of these days.
The goats are cleverer than anybody credits and I have been saying so since before you were born.
The wind takes the washing every time and every time somebody is surprised. Every time.
That plum fruits on the leeward side only. Everybody here will explain why and none of them are right.
Sums in the morning, letters after. Every child, every day. That was not true when I was a child.
It is colder up here. People inform me of this. I have lived here for sixty-one years.
This village is here because the one below it went under. That is the entire reason for the place.
We write down where the water reached each year. The date, the height, and who measured it.
From the top field you can see the sea and it is nearer than the drawing in the hall has it.
Nobody builds below the third post. It is a rule, it has a number, and I helped write the number.
Their family came up four generations back and we still call them the new ones. We always will.
The old road climbs up here and stops at nothing, because the something is under the water.
You can see the stilt village from here. They are on sticks. We are on rock. They think we ran.
We did run. That is the thing nobody up here will say. We ran, and we were right, and it still stings.
The ledger has every house lost, the year, the family, and what they managed to carry out.
It does not say that Vell's wife sang while she gutted fish, in a voice like a gull with a grievance.
Nobody was measuring the singing. That is the flaw in every ledger ever kept and I have not solved it.
Sabra carried plum stones up here in her mouth because both her hands were full. Four stones, two trees.
She is under the smaller one and the smaller one is the one that fruits. Make of that what you like.
There are keys by that door for houses that have been underwater since before I was married.
One shelf of the ledger is a single year. One shelf. You can see it from where you are standing.
We keep a chair that came up from the low house. Nobody sits in it. Nobody will move it. It is just there.
Our terraces copy the mountain place, where they built well and did not drown, and we copied it badly.
We copied a drawing of a drawing. It shows on the third row every spring, and it will show next spring.
The record keeper argues the carved city with anybody who sits down. Do not sit down.
Carved, not built, therefore older than the water, therefore there was a before. That is his whole case.
He is right, and it is why people have started eating standing up in his house.
The markers all stand on high ground, which people take as proof the builders knew. It proves they could see.
The calendar stone predicts nothing. I have said that indoors for fifty years and outdoors never once.
Two of every book, then four. The children copy until their hands cramp and I do not apologise for that.
We are writing down the drowned villages before the last person who saw them dies. I am one of the four.
Four of us left who saw them. That is the entire reason everybody is suddenly in such a hurry with me.
The orchard planted this spring fruits in nine years. Somebody did that sum on purpose and told nobody.
The seed jars go into the cave where it is cold. Not to eat. To keep. There is an enormous difference.
The lowlanders will come up eventually and we have already decided where to put them.
We have not told them. Telling them would be an insult and not telling them is also an insult. Pick one.
Our job is remembering. It is a strange thing to be handed at the end and I have stopped resenting it.
Thin air, thin soup, thin walls. I have made that joke for fifty years and it stays true.
Ice on the bucket most mornings. We wash on the warm days and the warm days are not warm.
Two hours down and four hours up and it is the same path. Somebody explain that to me again.
We burn dung because nothing here grows tall enough to burn. You stop noticing after about a decade.
The animals come in before dark and dark is early and getting earlier, or I am getting slower.
There is nothing to farm, so we keep records. That is not a joke. That is genuinely the economy.
My fingers will not bend. So, talking. That is what is left and I am making the most of it.
From here you can see the whole coast and it is a different shape from the map on that wall.
Nobody up here worries about the level. That is the entire reason there are people up here at all.
If it reaches us it has reached everybody. That is the closest thing to comfort this village has.
The traders tell us which villages went under this year. It is a short list. It has never been empty.
Nobody redraws the map. Somebody pencils the new edge over the old edge every few years.
You can read that map like the rings of a tree. Eleven edges on it now. I drew two of them.
We came up two lifetimes ago and we are still the new ones and we will be the new ones forever.
The dead go into the rock. You cannot dig a grave in this ground and people have tried and given up.
A comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth share one niche and nothing says whose they were.
Three people, or one person's whole life. Nobody can tell now, and I have decided that is allowed.
I came up from a fishing village at nine years old and I have not touched a boat since.
There is a boat up here. On a mountain. Somebody carried it up. I know who and I will not say.
The oldest names in the record are all from one drowned place, all in the same hand. My grandmother's hand.
We eat out of a bowl from a house nobody alive has been inside. It is a good bowl. It gets used daily.
I still tie knots the coast way. I have not seen the coast in fifty-eight years and my hands have not forgotten.
High as the mountain terraces, half as clever. I have been saying that since before it was a saying here.
Pilgrims come up wanting salt. Always salt. It is for the walk along the great wall and it always has been.
They are looking for the break where the sea came through. Generations of them, at it, one after another.
There is no break. I say that at this table and nowhere a pilgrim could possibly hear me.
There is a man here who owns a drawing of the carved city and charges people to look at it.
It is a bad drawing. It is the only one. He has done very well and I have never once said anything.
The calendar stone is meant to say when it stops. Every pilgrim reads it differently and goes home certain.
The tomb is the one they all agree on. Even the arguing ones go quiet about the tomb. Even me.
We take in whoever comes up. There is a room kept ready and it is rarely empty for long now.
Nobody asks a new arrival what they left behind. That is not manners. That is a rule and it has teeth.
The record book has run out of pages twice and we made more pages both times, badly, and it held.
The children learn the old hand, the difficult one, so the earliest pages do not go silent.
Everything is copied into two sets and one set goes deep into the cave where it is dry.
We are planting trees at this height for the first time ever. Nobody knows if they will take. We planted them.
I want carrying down to see the sea once before I go. Nobody has said yes and nobody has said no.
I am not getting any lighter and they are not getting any younger and we all know how this ends.
Same temperature in here all year round. Outside does as it likes. In here does not, and never has.
The soot has built a stripe along the roof, thickest at the height of a walking adult. That is the real record.
Water drips into that basin and fills it by morning and has done since before anyone kept count.
Nobody carved that basin. That is the drip, being patient, for longer than this village has had a name.
The floor of the front chamber has been swept so long that it sits dished in the middle. Swept, not worn.
Nobody past the third lamp without telling somebody. That is the only rule down here worth the breath.
The air in here is the temperature the outside was four months ago. It runs late. Like me.
People have lived in here longer than anywhere. Longer than the villages by a very great deal.
The old entrance is underwater now and the fish go in and out of it. We use the upper one.
Things come in here when the low villages give up on keeping them dry. That is most of what is in here.
We moved the seed jars deeper in after a wet winter, on the grounds that deeper is drier. It worked.
There is a water mark on that wall from a flood so old nobody knows which flood it was.
Everybody's grandparents' things end up in here. Mine are on the fourth shelf and I put them there.
The stone does not move. People say that as comfort. It only means the stone is not what is moving.
The dead lie in the fourth chamber, feet towards the entrance, every one of them the same way.
The oldest lie deepest. Walking in is walking backwards through everybody who was ever here.
The seed jars are labelled by hand and partway along the row the handwriting changes.
The first hand stopped. The second hand carried on. That is the whole story, written in labels, on jars.
The second hand is mine. I was nineteen. I did not know I was starting anything.
Books are stacked spine out in the dry chamber and the ones about the sea have been read to pieces.
Somebody copied an entire book into the margins of another book, having run out of paper. That was me as well.
My mother's name is on a jar down here. She filled it. It is still sealed and it will stay sealed.
Ochre handprints run the low passage at the height of a walking adult. One line is smaller and keeps stopping.
A child, keeping up. Made to walk it, like all of them. Like all of you, when you were small.
Seven shapes are painted in a row on the deep wall. A triangle, a long line, a ring of arches, and four more.
Everybody agrees the triangle is the markers and the line is the wall. After that it becomes a fight.
There is a charcoal drawing of the arches with a water line ruled dead straight across it.
Under the line somebody wrote a number. Nobody agrees what it counts. I have a theory and I am keeping it.
The carved-city arguments happen down here because the echo makes everybody sound more certain.
Say carved, not built, in the dark, and it comes back at you sounding like proof. That is the whole trick.
A calendar of small squares is cut by the entrance and the squares run out four winters back.
Whoever was cutting them stopped. It was me. My hands went. Nobody has picked it up and nobody has asked.
The seed jars are in two sets now. The back set is sealed with wax and it is not for us.
You may ask who the back set is for. I will answer, and then we shall both have to sit with it.
There is a new shelf down here, planed smooth and pegged in, empty, built to the size of books.
Somebody measured a future and made furniture for it. That is either the best or the worst thing in this cave.
The copying is done in here because it is dry. Two of everything, then four, then deeper in, then sealed.
The children are taught the way out in the dark now, by hand, by count of turns. That is a lesson.
